# Tusk documentation

Every page of tusk's user docs in one file: the README, the guides in docs/guide/ and the CLI reference in docs/cli/. Each page starts with a heading that names its path, and its relative links point at GitHub. `make docs` writes this file from those pages, so edit them rather than this. llms.txt indexes the same pages.

# README.md

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/README.md

# Tusk

**Agent memory you can code-review.**

Tusk indexes a folder of markdown into a typed, searchable graph that your agents query over MCP. The memory stays plain files in git, so every change an agent makes shows up in a diff, and `tusk doctor` fails the build when a link dangles or one of your conventions breaks.

<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/assets/tusk-web-dark.png">
  <img alt="tusk web's reading view: a plain-English search ranks this repo's package docs by similarity, and the best match is open beside the results" src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/assets/tusk-web-light.png">
</picture>

[Why tusk](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/README.md#why-tusk) · [Install](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/README.md#install) · [Try it](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/README.md#try-it-on-tusks-own-docs) · [Your own notes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/README.md#use-it-on-your-own-notes) · [Connect your agent](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/README.md#connect-your-agent) · [For agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/README.md#if-youre-an-agent-setting-this-up) · [How it compares](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/README.md#how-it-compares) · [Docs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/README.md#documentation)

## Why tusk

Agents write a lot: specs, plans, notes, decisions. Most agent-memory servers keep it in a database or a hosted store, where you can't diff or review it. Tusk keeps it where your team already reviews things.

- Every memory is a markdown file in git. You can review, revert or blame what an agent wrote, and Obsidian, vim and grep read the same files.
- `tusk.toml` declares node types, properties and edge types. A file that breaks the schema is still indexed, and `tusk doctor` reports it.
- Your conventions become checks. A rule is a filter that should match nothing, such as "a product note outside `docs/product/`". Doctor runs every rule and exits 1 when one matches, so a broken convention can fail CI.
- Hybrid search filters by structure, ranks by meaning with local Ollama embeddings, and returns the matching section with its heading and line range, so the agent reads a few lines instead of whole files.
- It runs locally: one Go binary and one SQLite file in `.tusk/`, with no account or hosted service.

### One query instead of grep and read

Say an agent needs to know how embedding prefixes work in this repo. `grep -ril prefix docs/packages` matches 7 files, about 60 KB to read. One hybrid query returns the section that answers it (output trimmed):

```console
$ tusk query 'type=package' --semantic "how are embedding prefixes applied to queries and documents" --take 1 --json
```

```json
[{
  "id": "docs/packages/embed",
  "title": "internal/embed — semantic indexing",
  "score": 0.83,
  "matched_units": [{
    "heading": "Public surface",
    "lines": [12, 21],
    "snippet": "…payload), and Header(node) apply the [embeddings] prefixes and header mode. EmbedQuery is the query-side entry point that applies the query prefix."
  }],
  "units_total": 3
}]
```

Over MCP it's the `tusk_query` tool with the same arguments. That's one example. Across 40 questions about these docs, an agent using `tusk_query` cited the right section every time (91% with grep and read) and made one tool call fewer, but read 11% more input tokens. A query result is about 8 KB, so tusk pays off on questions where grep has to dig. On a larger, private vault of 79 files, tusk read 17% fewer input tokens and finished 28% faster. [Benchmarks](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/guide/benchmarks.md) has the numbers, including the questions where tusk lost.

### Conventions that fail the build

```toml
[rule.domain-matches-directory]
description = "a product note lives under docs/product/"
filter      = "type=note AND domain=product AND NOT path=docs/product/**"
```

```console
$ tusk doctor
doctor: 2 errors, 0 warnings, 0 advice
  error    [dangling-edge] docs/product/refunds: edge "references" -> "docs/product/refund-policy" (target missing); also in #S1, #S1P1
  error    [rule:domain-matches-directory] docs/technical/billing: a product note lives under docs/product/
…
$ echo $?
1
```

[Rules and doctor](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/guide/rules-and-doctor.md) covers the rule grammar, severities and a CI recipe.

## Install

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/install.sh | sh
```

This downloads the latest release for macOS, Linux or Windows (amd64 or arm64) into `~/.local/bin`. With Go 1.26+ you can run `go install github.com/germanamz/tusk/cmd/tusk@latest` instead. Semantic and hybrid search need [Ollama](https://ollama.com) running locally with an embedding model (`ollama pull nomic-embed-text`). Everything else works without it.

Updating (`tusk update`), pinning a version and building from source are in [docs/guide/install.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/guide/install.md).

## Try it on tusk's own docs

This repo is a tusk vault: `docs/packages/` holds one typed page per Go package.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/germanamz/tusk && cd tusk
tusk reindex      # builds .tusk/ in about 10 seconds, embedding with Ollama if it's running
tusk web --open   # graph and reading views at http://127.0.0.1:7373
tusk query 'type=package' --semantic "what happens when the index gets corrupted"
```

Without Ollama, reindex still builds the graph, and its summary says how many nodes are left to embed.

## Use it on your own notes

Point it at the folder you already have:

```bash
cd ~/notes
tusk init --name notes   # finds your markdown and indexes it as notes
tusk reindex
tusk web --open
```

When the folder already holds markdown, `init` says how many files have no `type:`, adds the `vault` pack (note, meeting and decision types, plus wikilink edges) and sets `default-type = "note"` in `tusk.toml`. Every file then indexes as a note without being edited: its path, minus the extension, is its id, its first `# ` heading is its title, and its wikilinks become edges in any of the forms Obsidian writes: by name (`[[other-note]]`), as a path (`[[folder/other-note]]`), or relative to the note (`[[../folder/other-note]]`).

Frontmatter can still give a file another type and properties:

```markdown
---
type: decision
title: Use SSO
---

# Use SSO

Builds on [[notes/auth-rfc]].
```

Pass `tusk init --no-adopt`, or delete `default-type` from `tusk.toml`, to index only files with a `type:`.

[Workspaces, nodes and the manifest](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/guide/workspace.md) covers types, edges, type packs and what gets indexed.

## Connect your agent

The server is `tusk mcp` over stdio. It finds the vault by walking up from its working directory to the nearest `tusk.toml`, so the client has to start it inside the vault. Clients differ on that.

**Claude Code.** Run this in the vault:

```bash
tusk claude install
```

It installs a project plugin that runs the MCP server and gives each session a short orientation to the vault ([details](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/guide/mcp.md#the-claude-code-plugin)). For the server alone: `claude mcp add tusk -- tusk mcp`.

**Codex CLI.** `codex mcp add tusk -- tusk mcp`. Codex starts the server in the directory you launched it from. To pin one vault, set `cwd` in `~/.codex/config.toml`:

```toml
[mcp_servers.tusk]
command = "tusk"
args    = ["mcp"]
cwd     = "/path/to/vault"
```

**Gemini CLI.** `gemini mcp add tusk tusk mcp` writes `.gemini/settings.json` in the current project. Gemini also starts the server in the launch directory, and accepts `cwd` the same way.

**VS Code.** `.vscode/mcp.json` in the vault. VS Code starts the server in the workspace folder.

```json
{ "servers": { "tusk": { "type": "stdio", "command": "tusk", "args": ["mcp"] } } }
```

**Cursor.** `.cursor/mcp.json` in the vault:

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "tusk": { "command": "tusk", "args": ["mcp"] } } }
```

Cursor doesn't document which directory it starts servers in. If the server fails with `no tusk.toml found`, use the wrapper below.

**Zed.** In your settings. Zed starts the server in the project root.

```json
{ "context_servers": { "tusk": { "command": "tusk", "args": ["mcp"] } } }
```

**Claude Desktop, Windsurf, and clients with no project folder.** Wrap the command so it changes into the vault first (macOS and Linux):

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "tusk": { "command": "sh", "args": ["-c", "cd /path/to/vault && exec /absolute/path/to/tusk mcp"] } } }
```

Claude Desktop starts servers with a minimal `PATH`, so give tusk's absolute path (`which tusk` prints it). A `--workspace` flag that makes the wrapper unnecessary is [#794](https://github.com/germanamz/tusk/issues/794).

The server's tools, and why agents should prefer them over the CLI, are in [docs/guide/mcp.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/guide/mcp.md).

## If you're an agent setting this up

None of these commands prompt.

1. Install: `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/install.sh | sh` puts `tusk` in `~/.local/bin`. If `tusk --version` fails afterwards, that directory isn't on `PATH`.
2. Create the workspace in the vault root: `tusk init --name <name>`. It exits 1 if `tusk.toml` already exists, which you can treat as already done. If the folder holds markdown without a `type:`, init adds the vault pack and sets `default-type = "note"` so those files index as notes, and says so in its output; `--no-adopt` skips this.
3. Declare types, unless init already added the vault pack: `tusk pack add vault` adds note, meeting and decision types. Built-in packs ship inside tusk, so it works offline. It exits 1 if run twice (`--force` overwrites). Or write `[node-types.*]` in `tusk.toml` yourself.
4. Index: `tusk reindex`. If its summary ends with `queued for embedding (embedder unreachable)`, Ollama isn't reachable: the graph was built, and only semantic search is missing. It still exits 0.
5. Connect the client as described in [Connect your agent](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/README.md#connect-your-agent). For Claude Code, run `tusk claude install`.
6. Verify: `tusk status` prints node counts by type, so non-zero counts mean files were indexed. `tusk doctor` exits 0 when the vault is healthy and 1 when an error is present, listing errors first.

Commands exit 0 on success and non-zero on failure. `tusk query`, `node list`, `node get`, `edge list`, `context` and `run` take `--json`. `tusk reset` asks for confirmation unless you pass `--yes`. Once the MCP server is connected, use the `tusk_*` tools instead of the shell, and call `tusk_help` for the filter grammar and workflows.

A prompt you can paste into your agent:

> Install tusk (https://github.com/germanamz/tusk) and set it up for this folder. Follow the "If you're an agent setting this up" section of its README, connect it as an MCP server for this client, then run `tusk status` and `tusk doctor` and show me the output.

## How it compares

**grep and ripgrep** need no setup and are exact when you know the words. Tusk adds search by meaning, a schema, and links you can query. It costs an index, and Ollama for semantic search.

**Obsidian** is a good editor for the same kind of vault, and the two can share a folder: Obsidian for writing, tusk for agents and checks. Tusk resolves the links Obsidian writes, short names included, and `tusk node move` keeps them pointing where they did.

**A vector database or RAG pipeline** scales further, with more embedding models and hosted options. Tusk's index is derived from files you can read and review, and structure (types, edges, rules) is queryable in the same call as similarity. Tusk only talks to Ollama today.

**Agent-memory MCP servers** are easier to start with, because the agent just writes memories. Most keep them in a database, a JSON file or a hosted service, which you can't diff, review or fix in an editor. Tusk asks for more upfront (a schema), and in return you can review the memory.

### Where tusk falls short

- Semantic search needs Ollama running locally. There's no hosted embedding provider yet.
- One writer at a time per workspace: an advisory lock serializes writes from the CLI and the MCP server.
- Similarity ranking is brute-force cosine in memory. That suits a personal or team vault, not millions of documents.

# docs/guide/install.md

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/guide/install.md

# Installing and updating tusk

## Prerequisites

- (Optional, for semantic search) [Ollama](https://ollama.com) running locally with an embedding model, e.g. `ollama pull nomic-embed-text`. Everything except semantic and hybrid queries works without it.

## One-liner (prebuilt binary)

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/install.sh | sh
```

Detects your OS/arch, downloads the latest GitHub release, drops the `tusk` binary into `~/.local/bin` (override with `INSTALL_DIR=/usr/local/bin`), and installs its man pages into `~/.local/share/man` (override with `MAN_DIR`; `man tusk` works once that dir is on your `MANPATH`). Pin a specific release with `TUSK_VERSION=v1.1.0`. Prebuilt archives ship for darwin/linux/windows on amd64 + arm64.

## From source

Requires Go 1.26+.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/germanamz/tusk
cd tusk
make build
# binary at ./bin/tusk — move it onto your PATH
install bin/tusk /usr/local/bin/tusk
```

Or, without cloning:

```bash
go install github.com/germanamz/tusk/cmd/tusk@latest
```

Verify:

```bash
tusk --version
```

## Updating

If you installed a prebuilt binary, `tusk update` replaces it in place. Your workspace and `.tusk/` index are untouched.

```bash
tusk update              # latest release
tusk update v1.2.0       # pin a version (or roll back to one)
tusk update --check      # report what's available, change nothing
```

The archive is verified against the release checksums before anything is extracted, and the previous binary is kept aside until the replacement is in place, so a failed swap rolls back rather than leaving you with no binary. Man pages are refreshed alongside it.

A binary managed by Homebrew, installed with `go install`, or built from source is owned by that tool, so `tusk update` refuses it and prints the right command instead (`--force` overrides):

```bash
# From source
cd tusk && git pull && make build && install bin/tusk /usr/local/bin/tusk

# go install
go install github.com/germanamz/tusk/cmd/tusk@latest
```

Re-running the install one-liner also still works, and remains the way to bootstrap a machine that has no `tusk` yet:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/install.sh | sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/install.sh | TUSK_VERSION=v1.2.0 sh
```

After a major upgrade, run `tusk reindex` to pick up any indexer changes, then `tusk doctor` to confirm the workspace is healthy.

# docs/guide/workspace.md

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/guide/workspace.md

# Workspaces, nodes and the manifest

A Tusk workspace is just a directory:

```
my-brain/
├── tusk.toml                # workspace manifest (committed)
├── .tusk/                   # gitignored — local SQLite index
│   └── tusk.db
├── .gitignore
├── notes/
│   └── auth-rfc.md
├── tickets/
│   └── fix-login-bug.md
└── tags/
    └── auth.md
```

## Nodes are markdown files

Every `.md` file with a `type:` field in YAML frontmatter is a **node**. The file path (minus the extension) is the canonical **node id** — no separate id field.

```markdown
---
type: ticket
title: Fix login bug
status: active
priority: high
due: 2026-05-15
parent: tickets/auth-epic
blocks: [tickets/refactor-storage]
tags: [auth, security]
---

# Fix login bug

The bug occurs when users with SSO accounts hit the password reset flow.
See [[notes/auth-rfc]] for context.
```

- `type` is the only universally reserved key.
- Other frontmatter keys are either **properties** (string / int / date / enum / ref / list-of) or **edges** (declared in `tusk.toml`).
- `[[notes/auth-rfc]]` body wikilinks materialize as edges to that node id for any edge type declared with `wikilinks = true` (e.g. the `vault` pack's `references` edge). The Obsidian aliased form `[[notes/auth-rfc|the auth RFC]]` links to the same node id — the text after `|` is display only — and a `tusk node move` retargets the id while keeping the display text. A wikilink inside inline code or a code block is an example, not a link: it makes no edge, and a move leaves it as written. [Wikilinks](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/guide/workspace.md#wikilinks) covers the other ways a link can name its note.

### Wikilinks

A wikilink names its note in one of three ways, the same three Obsidian's "New link format" setting writes:

- **A path**, `[[notes/auth-rfc]]`, is the node id: the file's workspace path without `.md`.
- **A relative path**, `[[./auth-rfc]]` or `[[../notes/auth-rfc]]`, starts from the linking note's folder.
- **A name**, `[[auth-rfc]]` or `[[Auth RFC]]`, has no folder at all. A note whose id is exactly that name wins, so every link that resolved before names existed resolves the same way. Otherwise tusk looks the name up among every file's name (the file name without its extension), and one match resolves the link. When two or more files share the name, the link stays unresolved and `tusk doctor` reports an `ambiguous-wikilink` error with the files, so you can write the path of the one you meant.

Names match in any letter case by default, as Obsidian does. To match only the case a file name is written in:

```toml
[workspace]
link-case = "sensitive"   # default "insensitive"
```

Paths always match exactly. A `#S1` fragment still addresses a section of the note it follows (`[[auth-rfc#S1]]`). A heading-text fragment such as `[[auth-rfc#Some heading]]` does not resolve yet ([#808](https://github.com/germanamz/tusk/issues/808)), so that link dangles.

The same rules apply to a frontmatter value written as a wikilink, under an edge type (`relates-to: "[[auth-rfc]]"`) or a `ref` property. Names resolve once the whole workspace is indexed, so the order files are read in never matters, and a note added, removed or renamed outside tusk changes what a name finds on the next reindex without the linking files being re-read.

`tusk node move` keeps every link pointing where it did. A name stays as written while it still finds the moved note, so moving `auth-rfc.md` to another folder leaves `[[auth-rfc]]` alone; renaming the file rewrites it to the new name. When the move gives the note a name another note already has, the links to both notes become full paths, since the name alone would no longer tell them apart. Relative links are re-rendered from where each file lives after the move, the moved note's own included.

### Folders of plain markdown

Markdown without a `type:` is not a node, so an existing Obsidian vault or `docs/` folder indexes as an empty graph. Set a default type to index it as it is:

```toml
[workspace]
name = "notes"
default-type = "note"
```

Every `.md` or `.mdx` file with no type of its own (no frontmatter, or frontmatter without `type:`) is then indexed as a `note`. The type must be declared under `[node-types]`; the `vault` pack declares `note`. An adopted file takes its title from `title:`, then from its first `# ` heading, then from its file name, and any frontmatter it has still applies. HTML pages still need their `tusk:type` meta, since untyped HTML is usually build output.

Tusk never adds a type to these files. Reindex leaves them as they are, and `tusk node modify` writes frontmatter only when the change sets a property, so editing the body of a plain file keeps it plain. Changing or removing `default-type` re-processes every file on the next reindex, and files it no longer covers leave the index.

`tusk init` sets this up when the folder already holds untyped markdown: it reports how many files it found, adds the `vault` pack, and writes `default-type = "note"`. Pass `--no-adopt` to keep those files out.

## Edges connect nodes

Edges are typed, declared in the manifest, and can be created two ways:

- **Frontmatter** — the natural place. `parent: tickets/auth-epic` declares a `parent` edge.
- **CLI / MCP** — `tusk edge add --type blocks --source tickets/a --target tickets/b`.

Edge declarations enforce legality (`from`/`to` types), cardinality, ordering, and optional `acyclic = true` (cycles are rejected at write time). A hand-edited file that breaks `from`/`to` or cardinality is still indexed, and `tusk doctor` reports the edge as an error.

## Pages name the files they describe

Technical pages name source files, in inline code or as links. Set `paths = true` on an edge type and tusk records, with its line, each inline-code span that is a workspace-relative path (`` `server/ledger/core/service.go` ``, or a bare `Makefile`) and each link or image destination (`[the service](../server/ledger/core/service.go)`, resolved against the page's folder), so a file can find the pages that describe it:

```toml
[edge-types.describes]
from  = ["technical"]   # which pages are scanned
paths = true
```

With no `to`, the edge type holds no node edges, so its frontmatter values are paths too. `describes: [server/ledger/core/service.go]` declares the path outright, with no heuristic involved.

```bash
# Which pages name this file (or a directory above it), and where?
tusk query 'names-path=server/ledger/core/service.go' --include paths

# Only through one edge type, when several set paths = true
tusk query 'names-path:describes=server/ledger/core/service.go'

# Every path one page names
tusk node get technical/ledger --include paths
```

The source tree can stay in `[workspace] ignore`: a path ref targets a path, not a node. `tusk doctor` warns with `path-missing` when a page names a path that has been renamed or deleted, and the Claude Code plugin (`tusk claude install`) reminds the agent of those pages right after it edits the file.

## The manifest defines the schema

`tusk.toml` is the contract between you and the engine. A minimal manifest:

```toml
[workspace]
name = "my-brain"
ignore = ["bin/", "node_modules/", "*.test"]

[embeddings]
provider = "ollama"
endpoint = "http://localhost:11434"
model    = "nomic-embed-text"
dim      = 768

[node-types.note]
description = "A free-form markdown note"
properties = []

[node-types.decision]
description = "A captured decision"
properties = [
    { name = "decided-at",  type = "date", required = true },
    { name = "status",      type = "enum", values = ["proposed", "accepted", "rejected", "superseded"] },
    { name = "supersedes",  type = "ref",  to = "decision" },
]

[edge-types.references]
description = "Implicit edge materialized from body wikilinks"
from        = ["*"]
to          = ["*"]
cardinality = "many-to-many"
inverse     = "referenced-by"
```

`ref` properties auto-materialize edge types of the same name — declaring `supersedes` as a `ref` to `decision` gives you a `supersedes` edge for free.

Conventions the schema can't express, like "product notes live under `docs/product/`", are declared as rules that `tusk doctor` checks. See [Rules and doctor](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/guide/rules-and-doctor.md).

Edited `tusk.toml` while a daemon is running? `tusk reload` (or the `tusk_reload` MCP tool) re-reads and validates the manifest, hot-swaps the schema in place — no restart — and converges any sibling daemons via the `.tusk/manifest-epoch` sentinel. It then reindexes to re-validate your content against the new schema. Validation matches startup, so a reload lands the same state a restart would.

## Type packs (built-in templates)

Instead of declaring everything by hand, `tusk pack add <name>` splices a curated TOML block into your manifest:

| Pack | Adds |
|------|------|
| `vault` | `note`, `meeting`, `decision`; `references` (wikilinks) + `relates-to` |
| `tags` | `tag` node + `tagged` edge (with `tags: [a, b]` frontmatter shorthand) |
| `kanban` | `ticket` node with workflow-validated `status`; `parent` (WBS) + `blocks` edges |
| `dev` | `spec`, `plan`, `handoff`, `package` — dogfooding pack for tracking software projects |

Packs compose: add `vault` + `tags` + `kanban` and you have notes, decisions, tags, and a kanban workflow on top. `vault`, `tags` and `kanban` are compiled into tusk, so adding them by name works offline; `dev` installs by URL.

```bash
tusk pack add vault
tusk pack add tags
tusk pack add kanban
```

You can also load a pack from a URL or local file:

```bash
tusk pack add https://example.com/packs/research.toml
tusk pack add file://$PWD/my-pack.toml
```

## Indexing

The index lives in `.tusk/tusk.db` (SQLite + WAL). It is **derived state** — delete `.tusk/` and `tusk reindex` rebuilds it identically.

### One-shot reindex

```bash
tusk reindex
# Reindex done: 142 indexed, 0 removed, 3 skipped (2 not nodes)
```

`reindex` walks the workspace, parses every `.md`, validates frontmatter against the manifest, resolves refs + wikilinks into edges, and enqueues embeddings.

A skipped file is one reindex left out of the index. The `not nodes` count is plain markdown with no frontmatter or no `type:` (in a workspace without `default-type`), plus HTML with no `tusk:type`; these are fine and get no warning. Any other skip is a file reindex could not parse: it is logged as a warning and `tusk doctor` reports it.

### Live watcher

```bash
tusk watch
```

Runs fsnotify against the workspace and applies edits incrementally. Drains the embed queue in the background.

### What gets indexed

- Every `.md` file with a `type:` field, anywhere in the workspace, and every
  other `.md` file too when `[workspace] default-type` is set.
- Every `.html` / `.htm` file with a `<meta name="tusk:type">` tag — indexed
  over its **prose** (tags stripped, entities decoded), with `<meta name="tusk:*">`
  becoming typed node properties and `data-*` attributes captured as lenient
  signals under the reserved `data` key.
- Filtered through `.gitignore` + `[workspace] ignore` patterns.
- `.tusk/` and `.git/` are always ignored.

Off-schema content is **warned, not rejected** — a file with an unknown `type:`, a property violation, or an edge its edge type forbids still gets indexed (so it stays queryable) and surfaces in `tusk doctor`. The exception is a file reindex cannot parse at all (frontmatter that does not decode, say): it stays out of the index, and `tusk doctor` reports it as a `skipped-file` error with the parse error. Plain markdown with no frontmatter or no `type:` is not a node and is never reported.

## Architecture

Single Go binary, single SQLite index, single embedding provider (Ollama for now).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    workspace["Workspace<br/>(markdown + tusk.toml)"]
    engine["Engine (cmd/tusk + internal/*)<br/>manifest · node · edge · reindex · filter · embed<br/>watcher · behaviors · mcp"]
    db[".tusk/tusk.db<br/>(SQLite WAL, embeddings table)"]

    workspace -->|"fs walk / fsnotify"| engine
    engine -->|"reads / writes"| db
```

- **Filesystem > index, always.** The index is a cache; if it is stale, wedged, or corrupt, run `tusk reset` (or the `tusk_reset` MCP tool with `confirm: true`) to drop and rebuild it from your files. The markdown files are the source of truth, so nothing is lost.
- **Stateless across machines.** Clone the vault, reindex, get an identical brain.
- **Single-writer, many-readers.** SQLite WAL + a workspace-wide advisory lock so `tusk mcp` and one-shot CLI calls coexist.

Product vision and design principles live in [`PRODUCT.md`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/PRODUCT.md). Per-package notes live in [`docs/packages/`](https://github.com/germanamz/tusk/tree/main/docs/packages).

# docs/guide/querying.md

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/guide/querying.md

# Querying

Three query shapes run over the same index: a structural filter, semantic similarity, and hybrid, which filters and then ranks. The full filter grammar is in [`docs/cli/tusk_query.md`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_query.md), and agents can call `tusk_help(topic: "filter")`.

## Structural filter

A compact filter grammar that compiles to parameterized SQL. Property
comparisons accept `=` or `:` interchangeably; the rest of the grammar uses
the operators below.

```bash
# Property predicates (`=` and `:` are equivalent)
tusk query 'type=ticket status=active priority=high'
tusk query 'type:plan shipped-at>=2026-04-01'   # date ordering, chronological

# Path patterns on path and id: * stays in one folder, ** crosses folders
tusk query 'type=note path=docs/product/*'      # notes directly in docs/product/
tusk query 'path=docs/** path!=docs/archive/**' # all of docs/ except the archive

# Edge traversal: -> outgoing, <- incoming
tusk query 'type=ticket blocks->type=ticket'        # tickets that block other tickets
tusk query 'type=note references<- type=spec'      # notes referenced by specs

# The one term after the arrow constrains the linked node; group for more
tusk query 'type=note references->(domain=technical OR domain=wip)'
tusk query 'domain=product references-> NOT domain=product'   # product notes linking outside product

# Multi-hop
tusk query 'type=ticket parent->parent->title="auth-epic"'

# Sort + pagination
tusk query 'type=ticket status=active' --sort '+priority,-due' --take 10
```

## Semantic search

Requires `[embeddings]` configured (Ollama by default). Embedding runs asynchronously after writes; until a node is embedded, it's invisible to semantic queries (and surfaces in `tusk doctor`).

```bash
tusk query '' --semantic "auth bug in password reset flow" --take 5
tusk query 'path=docs/**' --semantic "billing totals"   # scoped to docs/ and below
```

Each result carries `matched_units`, the passages that matched, best first. A passage folds into its innermost section, so one finding is one row: the section's id, `heading`, and `lines: [start, end]`, plus the passage's score and snippet. Lines are 1-based and counted from the top of the file, frontmatter included, so an agent can open the file at the passage instead of reading all of it (HTML units carry no lines). `--max-units N` keeps the best N per file, MCP keeps 3 unless told otherwise, and `units_total` says how many there were. `[workspace] line-numbering` decides what ends a line: `lf` (the default, matching sed and grep -n), `universal` (adds a lone CR, like most editors), or `unicode` (adds the Unicode line separators).

### Matching the embedding model

Many embedding models are trained with an instruction prefix on each side, one for queries and another for documents. Ollama adds neither, so tusk lets you set them under `[embeddings]`, along with the chunk sizes and context window that suit the model:

```toml
[embeddings]
provider        = "ollama"
endpoint        = "http://localhost:11434"
model           = "nomic-embed-text"
dim             = 768
query-prefix    = "search_query: "
document-prefix = "search_document: "
```

| Model | `query-prefix` | `document-prefix` | Context window |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `nomic-embed-text` | `search_query: ` | `search_document: ` | 2K in Ollama |
| `embeddinggemma` | `task: search result \| query: ` | `title: {title} \| text: ` | 2K |
| `mxbai-embed-large` | `Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: ` | none | 512 |
| `snowflake-arctic-embed` (v1) | `Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: ` | none | 512 |
| `snowflake-arctic-embed2` | `query: ` | none | 8K |

Each prefix ends with a space. `{title}` in `document-prefix` becomes the note's title (`none` for sub-units). The other keys are `document-header` (`full`, `title`, or `none`: how much frontmatter leads each file chunk), `chunk-target-bytes` / `chunk-max-bytes` / `chunk-overlap-bytes` (defaults 1600 / 4000 / 200, sized for a 2K window; for a 512-token model set `chunk-max-bytes = 1000` and a smaller target such as `chunk-target-bytes = 800`, and consider `document-header = "title"` since the header doesn't count toward the cap), and `num-ctx` (passed to Ollama as `num_ctx`).

How much the prefixes matter was measured before they shipped ([#758](https://github.com/germanamz/tusk/issues/758)): a real vault of 79 markdown files, 44 hand-written queries with known target notes, note-level ranks scored from `tusk query --semantic --json`.

| Config | MRR@10 | hit@1 | hit@5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `nomic-embed-text`, no prefixes | 0.533 | 0.34 | 0.77 |
| `nomic-embed-text`, prefixes | **0.650** | **0.50** | **0.84** |
| `embeddinggemma-2`, no prefixes | 0.576 | 0.39 | 0.84 |
| `embeddinggemma-2`, prefixes | 0.532 | 0.34 | 0.80 |

The prefixes raised `nomic-embed-text` by +0.117 MRR@10 (paired bootstrap 95% CI +0.019 to +0.216), the only difference in the table that clears the noise. For `embeddinggemma-2` the recommended document prefix didn't help on that corpus. One vault isn't a general result, which is why the prefixes are settings and not a hard-coded table.

Which settings work best depends on the model and on your notes, so try a few semantic queries before and after a change. Changing `query-prefix` takes effect on the next query. Changing any other key re-embeds every note. Apply the change with `tusk reload` (or `tusk_reload` from an agent) so a running MCP server picks up the new settings too; `tusk reindex` also applies it, but a server that hasn't reloaded stops embedding until it does, rather than embed with the old settings. `tusk doctor` suggests the prefixes when it recognizes one of the models above with them unset, and names the missing one when only one of a two-sided pair is set. If you've tried a prefix and decided against it, set it explicitly to `""` (for example `document-prefix = ""`) and doctor stops suggesting it.

## Hybrid (recommended for agents)

Structural filter narrows the candidate set; semantic similarity ranks within it.

```bash
tusk query 'type=ticket status=active' --semantic "login flow" --take 10
```

## JSON output

Add `--json` to any query for structured output that's easy to pipe into an LLM or a script.

```bash
tusk query 'type=decision' --semantic "storage backend" --take 3 --json
```

# docs/guide/rules-and-doctor.md

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/guide/rules-and-doctor.md

# Rules and doctor

Types and edges say what a node may contain. `tusk doctor` checks the vault against them, plus any conventions you declare as rules, and exits 1 when it finds an error. That makes it something you can run after every agent edit, or in CI.

## Health checks

```bash
tusk status     # node counts, edge count, embed-queue depth, last reindex timestamp
tusk doctor     # health check; exits 1 when an error is present
```

Every doctor finding has a severity, and the report lists errors first. An `error` means the vault or the index is wrong: a dangling link, a property that breaks its declaration, a file reindex could not parse, a pinned id left behind by a rename. A `warning` means things are correct but degraded, such as a node missing from semantic results or a type you never declared. `advice` is a hint. `tusk doctor` exits 1 when an error is present, so you (or an agent) can run it after every edit and treat a non-zero exit as "I broke something". `--fail-on=warning` fails on warnings too; `--fail-on=never` always exits 0.

`doctor` is also the place to look when:

- semantic queries seem to be missing nodes → check the embed-queue depth and last error
- a wikilink points to nothing → a `dangling-edge` error names it
- a `[[name]]` wikilink matches more than one file → an `ambiguous-wikilink` error lists the files
- a manifest change just landed → re-validate every affected node
- a convention you declared as a `[rule.<name>]` is broken → each offending node is a `rule:<name>` issue

## Rules: conventions doctor checks

A vault usually has conventions on top of its types, like "product notes live under `docs/product/`". Write one as a filter that should match nothing:

```toml
[rule.domain-matches-directory]
description = "a product note lives under docs/product/"
filter      = "type=note AND domain=product AND NOT path=docs/product/**"

[rule.product-links-stay-in-product]
description = "a product page links only to product pages and the glossary"
filter      = "domain=product AND references-> (type=note AND NOT domain=product AND NOT id=docs/glossary)"
severity    = "warning"   # error (the default) | warning | advice
```

`tusk doctor` runs every rule and reports each matching node as a `rule:<name>` issue at the rule's severity, so a broken convention fails it like a dangling link would:

```console
$ tusk doctor
doctor: 2 errors, 0 warnings, 0 advice
  error    [dangling-edge] docs/product/refunds: edge "references" -> "docs/product/refund-policy" (target missing); also in #S1, #S1P1
  error    [rule:domain-matches-directory] docs/technical/billing: a product note lives under docs/product/
…
$ echo $?
1
```

The filter is the same grammar `tusk query` takes, so you can try it there first. Two differences: a rule matches file nodes only (sub-units share their file's `path`) unless the filter selects a sub-unit type such as `type=section`, and a rule's filter must name declared types, properties and enum values, because a typo there would match nothing and pass forever. A rule that fails those checks doesn't stop anything from loading; `tusk reload` lists it under warnings and `tusk doctor` reports it as a `rule-invalid` error.

## Running doctor in CI

`.tusk/` is gitignored, so a CI runner starts without an index, and doctor checks the index, not the files. `tusk doctor --reindex` builds the index from the checkout and then checks it. That pass skips embedding, so the runner doesn't need Ollama. On GitHub Actions:

```yaml
- name: Install tusk
  run: |
    curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/install.sh | sh
    echo "$HOME/.local/bin" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"
- name: Check the vault
  run: tusk doctor --reindex
```

Without `--reindex`, doctor on a fresh checkout reports an `index-not-built` warning rather than a clean vault. A warning exits 0, so add `--fail-on=warning` if you want a forgotten flag, or any other warning, to fail the job.

`tusk reindex` also works on a runner. When it can't reach Ollama it still builds the index, says how many nodes are left to embed, and exits 0. Pass `--no-embed` to skip embedding, or `--strict-embed` to make an unreachable embedder fail the run.

# docs/guide/mcp.md

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/guide/mcp.md

# The MCP server and the Claude Code plugin

`tusk mcp` runs an MCP server backed by the same indexing engine as the CLI, exposing the graph verbs as tools. Agents should prefer these tools over shelling out to `tusk`: they run in the warm daemon with the index already open. Stdio is the default transport; SSE is available on a loopback port.

```bash
tusk mcp                                          # stdio (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, …)
tusk mcp --transport sse --addr 127.0.0.1:8765    # SSE
```

It holds the workspace open for the lifetime of the session: a single SQLite handle, an embed-queue drainer, and an fsnotify watcher all live in the same process so the index stays warm across tool calls.

The server finds its workspace by walking up from its working directory to the nearest `tusk.toml`, and exits with `no tusk.toml found` when there isn't one. Per-client configuration, including which clients start the server in your project folder, is in the README under [Connect your agent](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/README.md#connect-your-agent). A `--workspace` flag for clients that can't set a working directory is tracked in [#794](https://github.com/germanamz/tusk/issues/794).

## The Claude Code plugin

Run this once in the workspace root (or pass `--claude` to `tusk init`):

```bash
tusk claude install
```

It writes a Claude Code plugin to `.claude/skills/tusk/`, which Claude Code loads for any session started in that folder. The plugin does two things:

- It runs the tusk MCP server, so the agent has the `tusk_*` tools. Claude Code holds a project plugin's server until each user approves it, so install approves it for you in `.claude/settings.local.json`, your uncommitted per-user settings. If `.mcp.json` already runs a tusk server, install removes that entry so the tools aren't registered twice.
- When a conversation starts, it adds a `tusk` block to the first message, next to CLAUDE.md. The block opens with a short orientation (the declared node types with counts, edge types, aliases, whether the index is current), followed by the `[context]` digest when `tusk.toml` declares one. `/clear` and compaction read it again. It's capped at `[context] max-bytes` (16384 by default); over that, alias sections go first, then recent nodes, then pinned ones. Run `tusk claude context` to see exactly what a session gets.

When an edge type sets `paths = true`, the plugin also reminds the agent of the pages that name a file right after it edits that file (see [path refs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/guide/workspace.md#pages-name-the-files-they-describe)).

The plugin folder can be committed, so teammates get it on clone if they have `tusk` on their PATH. Each of them approves the MCP server once, by running `tusk claude install` or in `/mcp`. Run `tusk claude install` again after upgrading tusk, because sessions warn when the plugin is older than the binary. `tusk claude status` reports what's installed, and `tusk claude uninstall` removes it.

To wire up only the MCP server by hand:

```bash
claude mcp add tusk -- tusk mcp
```

## Available MCP tools

| Tool | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `tusk_status` | node counts by type, edge count, queue depth, last reindex |
| `tusk_doctor` | health check: every issue has a severity (`error` / `warning` / `advice`); `error_count > 0` means something is broken |
| `tusk_node_get` / `tusk_node_list` | read by id or filter |
| `tusk_node_render` | render a node's content as plain text (HTML tags / markdown markup stripped) |
| `tusk_node_create` / `tusk_node_modify` / `tusk_node_move` / `tusk_node_delete` | write |
| `tusk_edge_add` / `tusk_edge_remove` / `tusk_edge_list` | edge CRUD |
| `tusk_query` | structural + optional `semantic` ranking |
| `tusk_context` | composed warm-context digest (pinned nodes, recent activity, aliases) |
| `tusk_run` | invoke a manifest-declared alias by name |
| `tusk_reindex` | force a full walk |
| `tusk_reload` | hot-reload `tusk.toml`: validate + swap the schema, no restart |
| `tusk_reset` | drop and rebuild the index from files (`confirm: true`) |
| `tusk_pack_add` | merge a built-in type pack's node/edge types into `tusk.toml` and hot-reload the schema |
| `tusk_help` | overview and topic deep dives (workflow, node-types, edge-types, manifest, filter, query, packs) |

Workspace bootstrap (`tusk init`), the Claude Code plugin (`tusk claude …`) and the web app (`tusk web`, graph + reading views) stay CLI-only.

# docs/guide/benchmarks.md

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/guide/benchmarks.md

# Benchmarks

Does an agent spend less to answer a question with `tusk_query` than with grep and read? To find out, Claude Code answered 40 questions about tusk's own package docs, three times with grep and read and three times with `tusk_query` and read, and the harness counted what each run spent.

With tusk, the agent cited the right section on every run (91% with grep) and made one tool call fewer per question (2 against 3). It also read 11% more input tokens per question and cost 37% more, and took the same time. On this corpus tusk buys accuracy, not tokens. A query result runs about 8 KB, where a grep result runs under 1 KB, so tusk comes out ahead only on questions where grep has to dig.

A second, larger corpus came out the other way on tokens. On a private vault of 79 files, tusk read 17% fewer input tokens, made two tool calls fewer and finished 28% faster, and accuracy was about the same. See [A second corpus](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/guide/benchmarks.md#a-second-corpus).

## Results

| | grep and read | `tusk_query` and read | tusk against grep, per question |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Input tokens | 17,108 | 20,809 | 1.11× (0.91–1.41) |
| Tool calls | 3 | 2 | −1 (−1 to 0) |
| Tool output | 7.6 KB | 10.4 KB | 1.41× (1.18–2.11) |
| Time | 7.7 s | 7.7 s | 0.99× (0.84–1.10) |
| Cost | $0.024 | $0.033 | 1.37× (1.26–1.64) |
| Cited the right section | 91% | 100% | +9 points (+2 to +17) |
| Judged correct | 98% | 100% | +2 points (0 to +7) |

The first two columns are medians over questions, taking each question's median run. The last column compares the arms question by question: the median of tusk's ratio (or difference) to grep, with a 95% confidence interval in brackets. A 1.11× ratio whose interval runs from 0.91 to 1.41 means tusk probably reads somewhat more, and the benchmark can't rule out no difference.

<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/eval/results/2026-10-14-tusk-docs/charts/tokens-tusk-vs-grep-dark.svg">
  <img alt="Input tokens per question, tusk against grep, on a log scale: tusk reads less on 16 questions, by up to 72%, and more on 24, by up to 2.75 times" src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/eval/results/2026-10-14-tusk-docs/charts/tokens-tusk-vs-grep-light.svg">
</picture>

<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/eval/results/2026-10-14-tusk-docs/charts/per-arm-dark.svg">
  <img alt="Spread of input tokens, tool calls, tool output and time per question, by arm" src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/eval/results/2026-10-14-tusk-docs/charts/per-arm-light.svg">
</picture>

<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/eval/results/2026-10-14-tusk-docs/charts/accuracy-dark.svg">
  <img alt="Share of runs that cited the right section and that the judge marked correct, by arm and question kind" src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/eval/results/2026-10-14-tusk-docs/charts/accuracy-light.svg">
</picture>

Splitting by question kind doesn't change the picture. On lexical questions, which share a distinctive word with their section, tusk read 16.2k tokens to grep's 15.1k. On paraphrase questions it read 21.7k to 17.8k. Grep cited the right section on 93% of lexical runs and 88% of paraphrase runs; tusk did on all of them.

Some of grep's citation misses are near misses: a bullet name or a bold label cited as if it were a heading, or the file's title instead of the section under it. Tusk's results name the heading of each matched section, so its citations come out exact. The judge's verdict is the better measure of the answers themselves. It marked three grep runs wrong. Two of those said no flag makes a `path-missing` finding fail CI, missing `--fail-on warning`. It marked no tusk run wrong.

## Where tusk lost

Tusk read more input tokens than grep on 24 of the 40 questions. Three things account for it.

**Every query costs about 8 KB.** A `tusk_query` result has a median size of 8.4 KB. It holds five results, each with up to three matched sections, and every section carries its id, parent id, type, heading level, line range, ordinal and score around a snippet of about 150 characters. A Grep result has a median of 0.7 KB and a Read 2.9 KB. Input tokens count the whole context once per turn, so a big result early in a run is paid for again on every turn after it. On `lone-carriage-return-lines` (2.10×), both arms took one search and one read. Tusk's query found `linenum.md` right away, but returned 8 to 15 KB, where grep's search and read came to 2 KB together. `reload-parse-error`, `update-install-method` and `plugin-check-ci` go the same way, and most of the 1.2× to 1.6× losses are this.

**The agent reads the file anyway.** The snippets point at the answer but rarely contain it, so the agent follows up with Read: 73 of the 120 tusk runs read a file, against 92 of the 120 grep runs.

**A miss costs several queries.** The largest losses come from first queries that ranked other pages above the answer:

- `link-case-reprocess`, 2.75×: "link-case change forces full re-process of vault" ranked `doctor.md` and `pathref.md` above the `reindex.md` "Notes" section that holds the answer. The agent ran up to three more queries and read all of `wikilink.md` before it got there.
- `slow-browser-tab`, 2.57×: the first query's top five didn't include `webui.md` at all, and in two of the three runs the agent read `webapp.md` or `bookview.md` before finding it.
- `incoming-links-once` (2.45×) and `second-condition-after-traversal` (1.81×): the agent re-queried with different wording before reading.

Tusk won when grep had to dig. On `move-note-name-links` (0.28×), `path-missing-severity` (0.34×) and `session-summary-concurrency` (0.35×), the question's words (move, rename, exit, doctor, queries) match lines all over the corpus. Grep ran three to seven searches and read several sections, while one query landed on the section.

So the follow-ups to try are smaller query results (fewer fields per matched section, fewer sections by default), returning the matched section's text when it's short so the agent doesn't need a Read, and better ranking for long sections that cover several topics. This benchmark is how to tell whether they work.

## A second corpus

The same harness ran with the same model and settings on a private vault of 79 markdown files and 684 sections: more than twice the files and four and a half times the sections of `docs/packages`. Its 40 questions were written the same way, half lexical and half paraphrase. The vault isn't public, so only the numbers are published.

| | grep and read | `tusk_query` and read | tusk against grep, per question |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Input tokens | 20,186 | 12,446 | 0.83× (0.63–0.93) |
| Tool calls | 3 | 1 | −2 (−2 to −1) |
| Tool output | 8.2 KB | 9.7 KB | 1.18× (1.06–1.65) |
| Time | 9.2 s | 6.1 s | 0.72× (0.65–0.82) |
| Cost | $0.027 | $0.028 | 1.10× (0.90–1.18) |
| Cited the right section | 95% | 97% | +2 points (−4 to +8) |
| Judged correct | 97% | 93% | −3 points (−8 to 0) |

Tusk read fewer input tokens on 28 of the 40 questions and finished faster on 33. Most of the gap is on paraphrase questions: tusk read 12.5k tokens to grep's 26.5k, and made 1 call to grep's 4. On lexical questions it read 12.4k to 16.0k. A query still returns more than a grep does. On a bigger corpus, though, grep needs more searches and reads to land, and every extra turn pays for the whole context again.

Cost came out about even anyway, because of the prompt cache. Tusk's larger results are new text, written to the cache, and a cache write costs about 12 times a cache read. Tusk wrote a median of 5.3k tokens to the cache against grep's 4.3k, and read 11.3k from it against grep's 15.5k.

The judge marked tusk wrong a little more often, 93% against 97%, but the interval reaches zero. In both arms, most wrong verdicts were right answers with an added claim the reference contradicts.

## How it was measured

The harness is [`eval/agentbench`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/eval/README.md), and every run's raw record is in [`eval/results/2026-10-14-tusk-docs/`](https://github.com/germanamz/tusk/tree/main/eval/results/2026-10-14-tusk-docs).

**Corpus.** [`docs/packages/`](https://github.com/germanamz/tusk/tree/main/docs/packages): 34 markdown files, one per internal Go package, 164 KB and 149 headed sections. Each run gets a fresh copy. The grep arm's copy is plain markdown; the tusk arm's copy also has the index, built once by `tusk reindex` before any agent ran, with `nomic-embed-text` embeddings from a local Ollama.

**Questions.** [40 questions](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/eval/tasks/tusk-docs.jsonl), each with the section or sections that answer it, spread over 28 of the 34 files. Half are *lexical*: they share a distinctive word with their section, so a grep for it lands. The other half are *paraphrase*: they describe the situation in other words ("What happens when you rebuild the index while Ollama isn't running?"). The questions were written by reading the files, not by searching with either arm's tools, so neither arm picked its own questions.

**Arms.** Both run Claude Code 2.1.299 headless (`claude -p`) with Claude Sonnet 5.5, the same short system prompt (answer from the docs in this directory, cite file and heading) and the same JSON schema for the answer. They differ only in their tools:

| Arm | Tools |
| --- | --- |
| grep | Grep, Glob, Read |
| tusk | `tusk_query` (the MCP server from this repo at commit 1ab211a) and Read |

Claude Code runs with `--restricted` and `--strict-mcp-config`, so no user settings, other MCP servers or code-running tools reach either arm, and the harness checks every run's tool list against its arm. Each question ran 3 times per arm, 240 runs in all, in shuffled order, 4 at a time.

**What's recorded.** For every run: tool calls (not counting the final structured answer), input tokens, tool output in bytes, wall time and cost as Claude Code reports it. Input tokens are everything the model read across all turns, cached or not, so they measure context size independent of caching. They include Claude Code's own system prompt and tool definitions, about 3.6k tokens per turn for the grep arm and 4.1k for the tusk arm, whose MCP tool schema and server instructions add about 500.

**Scoring.** An answer cites the right section when one of its citations names a target heading in the target file, or a heading nested inside it. A judge model (Claude Haiku 5.5) then compares the answer with the text of the target section and marks it correct or not. A failed run counts as a miss on both.

**Statistics.** Each question's figure is the median of its 3 runs. Arms are compared question by question: the tusk ÷ grep ratio for each question, then the median ratio, with a 95% confidence interval from 10,000 bootstrap resamples over questions.

## Limits

- One model and two corpora, both small. On 34 files with distinctive names and headings, grep is hard to beat. On 79 files tusk already reads less. Larger vaults are untested.
- The questions were written by Claude, reading the files, and labeled lexical or paraphrase by the same hand.
- Cost depends on prompt-cache hits, which depend on how runs overlap. Input tokens don't, which is why they're the headline.

## Run it yourself

```bash
make build
go run ./eval/agentbench run --tasks eval/tasks/tusk-docs.jsonl --paths docs/packages \
  --out eval/results/$(date +%F)-tusk-docs
```

You need the `claude` CLI logged in and Ollama running with `nomic-embed-text`. [`eval/README.md`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/eval/README.md) covers the flags, running it on your own vault, and how to write questions.

# Tusk CLI reference

This reference is generated from the Cobra help text in `cmd/tusk/`.
Edit the help strings, then run `make docs`.

- **[Workflows](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/workflows.md)** — multi-command recipes (bootstrap, ingest,
  query, MCP wiring, health checks).

## Commands

- [`tusk`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk.md) — Local-first memory for agents: index a markdown + HTML vault into a graph
  - [`tusk claude`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_claude.md) — Install and inspect the Claude Code plugin for this workspace
    - [`tusk claude context`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_claude_context.md) — Print the context block the Claude Code plugin adds to a session
    - [`tusk claude install`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_claude_install.md) — Install the Claude Code plugin into this workspace
    - [`tusk claude refs`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_claude_refs.md) — Print the reminder the Claude Code plugin adds after an edit
    - [`tusk claude status`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_claude_status.md) — Report the Claude Code plugin installed in this workspace
    - [`tusk claude uninstall`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_claude_uninstall.md) — Remove the Claude Code plugin from this workspace
  - [`tusk context`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_context.md) — Compose a warm-context digest from the manifest [context] block
  - [`tusk doctor`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_doctor.md) — Check workspace and index health; exits 1 when an error is present
  - [`tusk edge`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_edge.md) — Manage edges between nodes (add, remove, list)
    - [`tusk edge add`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_edge_add.md) — Add a typed edge from one node to another
    - [`tusk edge list`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_edge_list.md) — List edges, optionally filtered by source, target, or kind
    - [`tusk edge remove`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_edge_remove.md) — Remove a specific edge by source, kind, and target
  - [`tusk init`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_init.md) — Initialize a Tusk workspace in the current directory
  - [`tusk mcp`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_mcp.md) — Run the long-running MCP server (stdio or SSE)
  - [`tusk node`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_node.md) — Manage individual nodes (create, get, render, list, modify, move, delete)
    - [`tusk node create`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_node_create.md) — Create a new node file and index it
    - [`tusk node delete`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_node_delete.md) — Delete a node file and remove it from the index
    - [`tusk node get`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_node_get.md) — Print the source file (markdown or HTML) for a node by id
    - [`tusk node list`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_node_list.md) — List nodes from the index, optionally filtering by expression
    - [`tusk node modify`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_node_modify.md) — Modify a node's frontmatter properties
    - [`tusk node move`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_node_move.md) — Atomically rename a node and rewrite all referring edges
    - [`tusk node render`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_node_render.md) — Render a node's content as plain text (tags / markup stripped)
  - [`tusk pack`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_pack.md) — Install and manage type packs
    - [`tusk pack add`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_pack_add.md) — Copy a type pack's declarations into tusk.toml
  - [`tusk query`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_query.md) — Run a structural, semantic, or hybrid query against the index
  - [`tusk reindex`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_reindex.md) — Walk the workspace and bring the index up to date with disk
  - [`tusk reload`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_reload.md) — Hot-reload the manifest (tusk.toml) without restarting the daemon
  - [`tusk reset`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_reset.md) — Drop the local index and rebuild it from source files
  - [`tusk run`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_run.md) — Run a manifest-declared alias by name
  - [`tusk status`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_status.md) — Print a one-screen workspace summary
  - [`tusk update`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_update.md) — Replace the running tusk binary with a published release
  - [`tusk watch`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_watch.md) — Watch the workspace for external edits and keep the index in sync
  - [`tusk web`](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_web.md) — Serve the unified web app: 3D graph + reading views

# docs/cli/workflows.md

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/workflows.md

# Tusk workflows

Multi-command recipes. Each recipe states an intent, then lists the commands
in order with one comment line above each.

For per-command reference, see [the CLI index](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/README.md).

---

## 1. Bootstrap a new vault

You have an empty directory and want a working Tusk workspace with a
sensible schema.

```bash
# Create tusk.toml and .tusk/
tusk init --name my-brain

# Seed it with a type pack (here: kanban; built in, so no network needed)
tusk pack add kanban

# Confirm the manifest is valid and the index is healthy
tusk doctor
```

After this, write markdown into the directory by any means — Tusk's
`tusk node create` is one option, but vim/Obsidian/an LLM writing files
work just as well.

---

## 2. Author with an external editor

You prefer your editor; you just want Tusk to keep up.

In shell 1, leave the watcher running:

```bash
# Foreground watcher — debounces edits and refreshes embeddings
tusk watch
```

In shell 2, edit files freely:

```bash
# Create or edit any .md file under the workspace
$EDITOR notes/2026-05-16.md

# After saving, the watcher has already picked it up.
# Confirm it landed in the index:
tusk status
```

---

## 3. Structural → semantic → hybrid query

The same intent expressed three ways teaches the grammar by contrast.
Suppose you want: "design notes about SQLite write contention."

```bash
# Structural: only matches if frontmatter literally tags it
tusk query 'type:note AND +design AND title.contains:sqlite'

# Pure semantic: a permissive filter, ranked by similarity in embedding space.
# (The positional filter is required; use 'type:note' to scope or '' for everything.)
tusk query 'type:note' --semantic 'sqlite write contention'

# Hybrid (recommended for agents): tighter filter, then rank
tusk query 'type:note AND +design' --semantic 'sqlite write contention'
```

---

## 4. MCP wiring for Claude Code

You want Tusk's CLI surface available to an agent over MCP.

```bash
# Verify the workspace is healthy first
tusk doctor

# Start the MCP server (stdio is the default; Claude Code launches this for you)
tusk mcp
```

Then add this to your Claude Code MCP config (full instructions in the
project README):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "tusk": {
      "command": "tusk",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

Most read/write CLI verbs have a 1:1 MCP tool of the same shape
(`tusk_node_create`, `tusk_query`, …). Workspace-bootstrap commands
(`tusk init`, `tusk watch`) are CLI-only.

### The agent retrieval loop (use the tools, not the shell)

Once wired, an agent should work through the MCP tools rather than `tusk …`
in a shell — the tools run in the warm daemon with the index already open,
where each `tusk …` shell call cold-starts a process and reopens the database:

1. `tusk_context` — pull the workspace's warm digest (pinned nodes, recent
   activity, named aliases) to orient.
2. `tusk_query` — structural + semantic retrieval; expand rows with
   `include: ["body", "edges"]` to avoid follow-up round-trips.
3. `tusk_node_get` — fetch a specific node by id when you need its full body.
4. `tusk_node_create` / `tusk_node_modify` / `tusk_edge_add` — write findings
   back as nodes and typed edges.

Reach for the shell only to bootstrap a workspace (`tusk init`) or open the
web app (`tusk web`, the local graph + reading views).

---

## 5. Health check and recovery

Something feels off — drift, dangling edges, or stale embeddings.

```bash
# See what's wrong
tusk doctor

# Catch the index up with disk
tusk reindex

# Re-run doctor to confirm
tusk doctor
```

---

## 6. Install a type pack

You want to add a built-in schema bundle.

```bash
# Copy the pack's node/edge type declarations into tusk.toml
tusk pack add kanban

# Inspect the manifest diff in your editor
git diff tusk.toml

# Verify the schema is still consistent
tusk doctor
```

If the pack collides with existing declarations:

```bash
# Force-overwrite the colliding sections
tusk pack add kanban --force
```

# docs/cli/tusk.md

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk.md

## tusk

Local-first memory for agents: index a markdown + HTML vault into a graph

### Synopsis

Tusk is a local-first memory system for coding agents. It turns a directory
of markdown and HTML files into a schema-validated, semantically-indexed graph and
serves that graph over MCP, so an agent recalls context with a single query
instead of many filesystem round trips.

Files are the source of truth (markdown and HTML + a tusk.toml manifest), git is
the history, and tusk is the indexer and retrieval engine. Every node is a plain
markdown or HTML file you can read, edit, and commit by hand — nothing is locked
away in a proprietary store.

WHY GRAPHRAG
  An agent that greps and reads files pays one round trip per file and still
  misses how they relate. Tusk indexes nodes, their typed edges, and vector
  embeddings up front, so a single "tusk query" (or the tusk_query MCP tool)
  returns the matching nodes plus their graph-expanded neighbours ranked by
  semantic similarity — the context an agent needs, gathered in one call.

HOW TO USE
  1. tusk init --name my-brain   Create tusk.toml and the .tusk/ index.
  2. edit tusk.toml              Declare node/edge types; "tusk reload" hot-swaps
                                 changes into a running daemon (no restart).
  3. tusk node create …          Add content (or write .md files directly).
  4. tusk reindex / tusk watch   Bring the index up to date / keep it live.
  5. tusk query / tusk context   Retrieve structurally, semantically, or both.
  6. tusk mcp                    Expose the same surface to an MCP agent.

  Most read/write verbs are also MCP tools (tusk_query, tusk_node_create, …),
  so an agent uses the same surface without a shell. Run "tusk doctor" any
  time to surface schema warnings, dangling edges, and index-health issues.

CONFIGURATION
  All configuration lives in tusk.toml at the workspace root:

    [workspace]              name, ignore globs, sub-units (default true)
    [node-types.<name>]      typed properties a node may/must set
    [edge-types.<name>]      from / to / cardinality / ordered / inverse /
                             acyclic / hierarchy / hierarchy-default /
                             wikilinks for typed relationships
    [embeddings]             provider = "ollama", model, endpoint, dim,
                             api-key, workers, timeout-seconds — enables
                             semantic search; query-prefix, document-prefix,
                             document-header, chunk-target-bytes,
                             chunk-max-bytes, chunk-overlap-bytes, num-ctx
                             match tusk to the embedding model (e.g.
                             nomic-embed-text: query-prefix "search_query: ",
                             document-prefix "search_document: ")
    [query.graph-expansion]  enabled, hops (1|2), edge-types, weight,
                             candidate-multiplier — tunes graphrag retrieval
    [graph.cluster]          by (type|property|ancestor|community), huddle,
                             hull, community-edges, resolution — cluster lens
                             for the "tusk web" graph view
    [context]                pinned, recent, include — shape the warm-context
                             digest produced by "tusk context"; max-bytes caps
                             the block "tusk claude" hands Claude Code
    [lease]                  ttl_seconds (default 60) for multi-instance
                             indexing
    [behaviors.<kind>]       manifest-declared behaviors
    [alias.<name>]           saved queries runnable via "tusk run <name>"

  Environment overrides (read once at startup, highest precedence):
    TUSK_EMBED_WORKERS       embed/reindex pool size; 0 = read-only instance.
                             Falls back to [embeddings] workers, then
                             max(1, NumCPU/2).
    TUSK_LEASE_TTL_SECONDS   lease window in seconds. Falls back to
                             [lease] ttl_seconds, then 60.

  See "tusk <command> --help" for per-command flags and detail.

### Examples

```
  # Bootstrap a fresh memory vault and verify it
  tusk init --name my-brain
  tusk doctor

  # Index markdown already on disk, then keep it live in the background
  tusk reindex
  tusk watch

  # Add a node (or just write the .md file yourself and reindex)
  tusk node create --type note --path notes/auth-design.md \
      --title "Auth design" --prop tag=architecture

  # Retrieve: structural, then semantic, then graph-expanded hybrid
  tusk query 'type=note AND tag=architecture'
  tusk query 'type=note' --semantic 'how does login work' --min-score 0.5
  tusk query 'type=note' --semantic login --graph-expand --hops 2 --include edges

  # Compose a warm-context digest for an agent session
  tusk context

  # Serve the graph to an MCP agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Zed)
  tusk mcp

  # Give Claude Code sessions in this vault its digest and tools
  tusk claude install

  # Run a read-only MCP instance that never drains the index
  TUSK_EMBED_WORKERS=0 tusk mcp
```

### Options

```
  -h, --help      help for tusk
  -v, --verbose   emit debug-level logs to stderr
```

### SEE ALSO

# docs/cli/tusk_claude.md

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_claude.md

## tusk claude

Install and inspect the Claude Code plugin for this workspace

### Synopsis

Manage the Claude Code plugin tusk ships for this workspace.

The plugin lives at <workspace>/.claude/skills/tusk/ and Claude Code loads it
for any session started in the workspace root. It carries two things:

  * The tusk MCP server ("tusk mcp"), so the agent has the tusk_* tools.
  * A hook that runs "tusk claude context" when a conversation starts and adds
    its output (a short orientation plus the [context] digest) to the first
    message, the way CLAUDE.md is added. /clear and compaction re-read it.
  * A hook that runs "tusk claude refs" after the agent edits a file and,
    when vault pages name that file in inline code or a link (edge types
    with paths = true), adds a short reminder listing them after the edit's
    result. Each file is mentioned once per session.

Run "tusk claude install" once per workspace (or "tusk init --claude"), and
again after upgrading tusk to refresh the plugin.

### Options

```
  -h, --help   help for claude
```

### Options inherited from parent commands

```
  -v, --verbose   emit debug-level logs to stderr
```

### SEE ALSO

* [tusk](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk.md)	 - Local-first memory for agents: index a markdown + HTML vault into a graph
* [tusk claude context](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_claude_context.md)	 - Print the context block the Claude Code plugin adds to a session
* [tusk claude install](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_claude_install.md)	 - Install the Claude Code plugin into this workspace
* [tusk claude refs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_claude_refs.md)	 - Print the reminder the Claude Code plugin adds after an edit
* [tusk claude status](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_claude_status.md)	 - Report the Claude Code plugin installed in this workspace
* [tusk claude uninstall](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_claude_uninstall.md)	 - Remove the Claude Code plugin from this workspace

# docs/cli/tusk_claude_context.md

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_claude_context.md

## tusk claude context

Print the context block the Claude Code plugin adds to a session

### Synopsis

Print the block the plugin adds to the first message of a Claude Code
conversation: a short orientation (the vault's declared node types with
counts, edge types, aliases, index state), then the [context] digest
("tusk context") when tusk.toml declares one.

The block stays within [context] max-bytes (default 16384). Over budget, it
drops alias sections first, then recent nodes, then pinned nodes, a whole node
at a time, and says so in its last line. The orientation is never cut.

It never fails a session: outside a workspace it prints nothing, a broken
tusk.toml prints a one-line notice, and a missing index prints the
orientation alone. It always exits 0.

```
tusk claude context [flags]
```

### Examples

```
  # Preview what a Claude Code session sees
  tusk claude context

  # Preview with a tighter budget
  tusk claude context --max-bytes 4096
```

### Options

```
  -h, --help            help for context
      --max-bytes int   override the block's byte budget ([context] max-bytes, default 16384)
```

### Options inherited from parent commands

```
  -v, --verbose   emit debug-level logs to stderr
```

### SEE ALSO

* [tusk claude](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_claude.md)	 - Install and inspect the Claude Code plugin for this workspace

# docs/cli/tusk_claude_install.md

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/germanamz/tusk/main/docs/cli/tusk_claude_install.md

## tusk claude install

Install the Claude Code plugin into this workspace

### Synopsis

Write the tusk plugin to <workspace>/.claude/skills/tusk/.

Install also approves the plugin's MCP server for you: Claude Code holds a
project plugin's MCP server until each user approves it, so install adds
"plugin:tusk:tusk" to enabledMcpjsonServers in .claude/settings.local.json
(your per-user, uncommitted settings).

If .mcp.json runs its own "tusk mcp" server, install removes that entry
(and the file, when it held nothing else) so the tools are not registered
twice. Pass --keep-mcp-json to leave it.

Re-running install is safe: it rewrites the files it owns. It refuses a
.claude/skills/tusk folder it did not write unless you pass --force.

The plugin runs the binary named by --bin, "tusk" on PATH by default. A
relative path resolves against the workspace root, where sessions start.

```
tusk claude install [flags]
```

### Examples

```
  # Install for this workspace
  tusk claude install

  # Point the plugin at a locally built binary
  tusk claude install --bin ./bin/tusk
```

### Options

```
      --bin string      tusk binary the plugin runs (default "tusk")
      --force           replace a .claude/skills/tusk folder tusk did not write
  -h, --help            help for install
      --keep-mcp-json   leave a .mcp.json tusk server in place
```

# docs/cli/tusk_claude_refs.md

## tusk claude refs

Print the reminder the Claude Code plugin adds after an edit

### Synopsis

Print the reminder the plugin adds after Claude Code edits a file: the
vault pages that name the file, or a directory above it, in inline code, a
link, or a frontmatter value, with the lines and sections they name it in. The pages that name the file itself
come first, then those naming a nearer directory. At most --max pages are
listed; a last line says how to see the rest.

Pages name paths through edge types that set paths = true in tusk.toml. The
path may be absolute or relative to the current directory; one outside the
workspace prints nothing.

The plugin calls this once per file a session edits. It never fails an edit:
when nothing names the path, the workspace declares no paths edge type, or the
index is missing, it prints nothing. It always exits 0.

```
tusk claude refs <path> [flags]
```

### Examples

```
  # Preview the reminder an edit to this file would trigger
  tusk claude refs server/ledger/core/service.go
```

### Options

```
  -h, --help      help for refs
      --max int   list at most N pages (default 5)
```
